cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant C such that, for every n≥2, every integer word length w≥⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every list x₁,…,xₙ∈{0,…,2ʷ−1}, the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most Cn?
cards.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
cards.why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.

importance.reason: A foundational algorithmic primitive whose optimal complexity tests the computational power of the word RAM and would affect many tasks built on ordering integer keys.

context_blocks.text: Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles w=O(log n). Divide each key into digits of about log₂n bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size O(n). There are O(1+w/log n) passes, giving O(n(1+w/log n)) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If w=(log n)^{3/2}, however, that same argument takes about √log n passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for w=Ω((log n)² log log n), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’s O(n√log log n), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic O(n log log n) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.

cards.title: Can all pairwise sums X+Y be sorted in quadratic time?
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer n≥2 and every X=(x₁,…,xₙ), Y=(y₁,…,yₙ)∈ℝⁿ, A outputs a permutation ((i₁,j₁),…,(i_{n²},j_{n²})) of [n]×[n] satisfying x_{i_r}+y_{j_r}≤x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}} for 1≤r<n², in at most Cn² unit-cost operations?
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.
cards.status_note: TOPP Problem 41, primary comparison and real-RAM sources, and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No uniform quadratic-time algorithm or matching impossibility result for the stated real-valued problem was found. The 2017/2018 decision-tree result does not settle total time. This is a source review, not an independent proof audit.

cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All n² index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of b=d⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for some fixed integer d≥3 chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ᵇ, quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by O(n log n) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the O(n²) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/n² ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.

context_blocks.text: The input is small compared with the output. For X=(0,3) and Y=(1,4), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are n² output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for n² unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix M_ij=x_i+y_j increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as M_ij+M_kl=M_il+M_kj. The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all n² sums takes O(n² log n) time. Writing the required output already takes Ω(n²) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that O(n²) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining O(n² log n) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained O(n log² n) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of X+Y. The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.

cards.definitions: A hypergraph H=(V,E,w) has E⊆{e⊆V:|e|≥2} and weights w:E→ℝ_{≥0}. Its cut value is cut_H(S)=Σ_{e∈E: e∩S≠∅ and e∩(V\S)≠∅}w(e): a crossing hyperedge contributes its weight once, independently of how many of its vertices lie on either side. Zero-weight edges may be discarded; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. Empty or singleton hyperedges never cross a cut and are omitted without loss. H′=(V,E′,w′) follows the same conventions, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights. The output edge set E′ need not be a subset of E, following the original problem statement; new vertices are not permitted. Size means |E′|, not Σ_{e∈E′}|e|, weight-encoding length or total storage bits. C is independent of n, ε, edge count, rank and all weights. The empty edge set is allowed, and a zero input cut must remain exactly zero. This is a finite-object existence question: no construction algorithm, running-time or probability guarantee is imposed.

context_blocks.text: A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge {1,2,3,4} of weight one contributes one to both the partition {1}|{2,3,4} and the partition {1,2}|{3,4}. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit O(n/ε²)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using O(n log n/ε²) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.
The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the Cn/ε² hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

cards.title: Can the final survivors of an offline heap sequence be found with linear comparisons?
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic comparison algorithm and an absolute constant C that, for every legal sequence of N insert and delete-min operations starting from an empty priority queue, determines exactly which inserted items remain after the entire sequence using at most CN key comparisons? The complete operation sequence and all inserted keys are available before computation begins. Only the final membership vector is required; the algorithm need not output the items removed at intermediate delete-min operations or their removal order.
cards.definitions: Each insert introduces a distinct item with a key in an opaque totally ordered universe; all inserted keys are pairwise distinct. A delete-min removes the currently present item of smallest key. Legality means that in every prefix the number of delete-min operations is at most the number of inserts. If I is the total number of inserts, the output is an I-bit vector in insertion order, marking exactly the items still present after all N operations. The algorithm may examine any part of the input sequence at any time. Its only access to key values is by pairwise order comparisons; operation positions and item identities carry no information about key order. Count every key comparison, including preprocessing comparisons. Ordinary computation on indices and comparison outcomes is not the cost measure, but the algorithm must terminate and be correct on every input.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a uniform deterministic algorithm meeting the CN comparison bound for every legal sequence, or prove that every such algorithm requires a superlinear number of comparisons on a family of inputs. Sorting all removed items or simulating the queue online would solve stronger tasks; a lower bound for those stronger tasks is not a negative answer here.
cards.why: This isolates a basic gap between maintaining a dynamic process and computing its final outcome. It connects offline data structures with selection and comparison lower bounds, in a small enough model that both algorithms and adversaries can be stated precisely.

importance.reason: A clean offline-versus-online information question for the priority-queue primitive. It could reveal a general way to avoid reconstructing unneeded intermediate outputs, while remaining narrower than model-wide dynamic lower bounds.

progress.text: Kozma explicitly asks whether final heap survivors can be computed in o(N log N), or even O(N), comparisons. The source identifies the all-insertions-first case as solvable by linear-time selection and notes that the usual sorting argument does not apply.

context_blocks.text: A usual priority queue must identify each minimum when the corresponding request arrives. The offline task can postpone every decision and return only a final set. For example, after insert(8), insert(2), delete-min, insert(1), the survivors are 8 and 1. This is not simply the set of the two largest inserted keys: 2 disappeared before 1 became available. The interleaving still matters even though the intermediate outputs are discarded.

One upper bound is to simulate a comparison heap and mark its remaining elements, using O(N log(N+2)) comparisons. At the other extreme, when all insertions precede all deletions, one linear-time selection suffices to find the surviving upper part of the key order. The question asks whether arbitrary temporal interleaving can be handled without losing that linear comparison bound.

The ordinary heap sorting lower bound depends on recovering the entire order of the extracted keys. Here, if I items were inserted, there are at most 2^I possible membership vectors. Counting outputs therefore does not give the usual factorial number of leaves needed for sorting. This observation only removes one lower-bound argument: a small output space by itself is not a construction of a shallow comparison decision tree.

A successful approach can exploit future deletions and later insertions, because the complete schedule is known. It need not maintain any particular heap representation. That freedom makes the problem a useful test of how much information an algorithm really needs when only a summary of a dynamic process is requested. The formulation deliberately asks about comparisons, leaving a linear total running time as a stronger goal.

cards.title: Can reachability diameter be approximated within a constant in near-linear time?
cards.formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least 2/3 in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving D(G)=0 on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
cards.why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.
cards.definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.

progress.text: Theorem 9 gives an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in near-linear time. Theorem 7 gives additive error $k$ in $O(nm/k)$ time; these guarantees leave the constant-factor near-linear target unresolved.

Corollary 5 conditionally excludes better-than-two approximation below the Boolean-matrix-multiplication exponent; its combinatorial version excludes truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms under combinatorial BMM. These results do not exclude every constant approximation.

references.authors: Ben Bals, Joakim Blikstad, Daniel Dadush, Yasamin Nazari, and Jonas Schmidt
references.locator: Definition in the introduction; Corollary 5, Theorems 7 and 9, Open Problem 1

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Open Problem 1 at ESA 2026; the near-linear constant-factor target is a focused part of that broader question.

context_blocks.text: A directed graph need not be strongly connected. Taking the maximum over all ordered pairs then produces infinity as soon as one pair is unreachable, concealing the lengths of the routes that do exist. Reachability diameter discards unreachable pairs. On a one-way path of five vertices it is four, even though most ordered pairs have no directed route.

A familiar undirected idea is to search from an arbitrary vertex and use a farthest vertex as a witness. Directionality breaks its guarantee. Consider a long one-way path and an extra sink reached by an edge from the first path vertex. Searching from that sink sees no other vertex; searching toward it sees only the first path vertex. Both searches reveal a distance of one while the reachability diameter can be arbitrarily large. This is an illustrative counterexample to that particular pivot choice, not a lower bound against every sampling algorithm.

There is also a distinction between additive and multiplicative error. An estimate within $k$ of the truth is useful when $D(G)$ is much larger than $k$, but gives little information when the diameter is small. The question requires a useful relative guarantee on every input, including graphs whose longest finite shortest path has only a few edges.
The 2026 paper makes this a fine-grained algorithmic question and leaves a substantial gap for unweighted graphs. Its strong hardness results for weighted graphs do not settle the unit-weight case.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
